transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I suppose what finally pushed me to come in is… I keep finding myself getting up when I’m meant to be sitting still. Like in staff meetings at school, everyone else is seated and I’ll suddenly decide I need to refill my coffee or check a handout at the back of the room. And it’s not really urgent, you know?

It happens at dinner too, which is embarrassing sometimes. I’ll pop up to get something or just move around, and then I realize everyone else has stayed put. I used to joke that teachers are just used to being on their feet all day, but lately it’s been bothering me enough that I thought I should ask someone about it.
When you get up like that, do you feel an inner restlessness or urge to move?

Yes, I think so… though I don’t always notice it as “restlessness” in the moment. It’s more like I suddenly just need to be up—refill my coffee in a meeting, go check something at the back of the room, that sort of thing. And then afterwards I realize nothing was actually urgent.

At dinner it’s similar. I’ll get up for something small, and then I notice everyone else is still sitting there. It reminds me of being at school, actually, because as a teacher you’re used to moving around the classroom all day, so I used to tell myself that was just normal. But yes, I suppose there is this urge to move before I’ve really thought it through.
Did this urge to get up and move start after you began taking a new medication or changed the dose of one?

I’m not sure, actually. I can’t think of a clear link like that. I mean, I’ve had the usual sorts of health bits over the years, and you know how sometimes one prescription changes and then you wonder if everything is connected—but with this getting-up thing, I haven’t really noticed it starting right after anything like that. It feels more like something I’ve just… done, and only recently started paying proper attention to.
When you were a child, were you often the one who had trouble staying seated?

Oh, yes, I think I was. My old report cards—my mother kept everything, in boxes, you know, birthday cards, school things, all of it—used to say I was bright, but that I couldn’t stay in my seat or wait my turn.

And my mum used to joke that before I was even ten, I’d worn a little path between my desk and the pencil sharpener because I was always getting up for something. At the time everyone just made it into a sort of funny family story, but looking back, yes, I suppose I was that child.
Are you currently taking any antipsychotic medicine?

I don’t think so… I mean, I’m not always brilliant with the names of medicines, to be honest. I tend to remember them by what the box looks like, which is probably not very helpful. But nothing that I’d think of as an antipsychotic, no—unless there’s something with another name I wouldn’t recognize.
Do you often have trouble focusing on what people are saying, even when you want to pay attention?

I’m not sure, honestly. I mean, I do try to listen—especially if someone’s telling me something important. In teaching you get used to tuning in to all sorts of voices at once, though actually that reminds me, staff meetings are a different matter entirely, because they can go on and on about timetables and someone’s always lost the minutes from last time…

Sorry, what was the exact question? Whether I lose track of what people are saying? I suppose I haven’t really noticed it as a major thing, not in a way I could confidently say yes to.
When you’re trying to sit still, do you find yourself repeatedly bouncing your legs or shifting your body because you feel you can’t keep still?

Yes, I do. Not in a dramatic way, but I notice it. If I’m sitting at my desk marking essays, I’ll suddenly realize I’ve been tapping my foot or clicking my pen for ages. Or in church—where of course you’re meant to be still and quiet—I’ll find myself shifting about in the pew and then I sort of tell myself, “For goodness’ sake, settle down.”

It’s funny, actually, because some essays take so long to get through, especially when they’ve all used the same phrase from the textbook and you start wondering whether you explained it badly in the lesson… sorry, yes—the short answer is yes, I do fidget like that.
When you have to stay seated, does it feel physically unbearable to remain still until you get up?

Yes—well, “physically unbearable” sounds a bit strong, but that’s sort of what brought me in, really. I keep finding reasons to get up when everyone else is still seated.

Like in meetings I’ll suddenly decide I need to refill my coffee, or check a handout, or walk to the back of the room for no especially good reason. And at dinner I might pop up to get something even when it isn’t urgent. I can tell other people are just sitting there normally, and I’m the one sort of… inventing a reason to move.
